title: Fast-Anything: Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow
abstract:
Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow. Rewriting a whole app in Rust costs months, minute-long compiles and gigabytes of target/ . Most of the runtime sits in a few functions anyway. fast-anything finds those functions, has your coding agent port only them to Rust, proves the port gives the same results on real recorded calls, and swaps it in. One command, fully reversible. Install npm i -g @el4cteo/fast-anything # or: cargo install fast-anything Ports are compiled with your Rust toolchain ( rustup ). Use fast-anything go --agent claude -- python app.py # or: -- node app.ts / bun app.ts / deno run -A app.ts / ruby app.rb / java App.java / mvn exec:java / gradle run / go run . / php app.php / clang -O2 main.c Or step by step: command what it does scan -- <cmd> profiles the app, ranks functions by time × how portable they are port [id] records up to 500 real calls, creates a one-function Rust crate + TASK.md verify release-builds the port and replays every recorded call enable / disable swaps the Rust in or out (one marked block, removed byte for byte) bench times the whole app, original vs Rust, interleaved runs report markdown + SVG card for your PR doctor checks Rust, your runtimes and your agents --agent takes claude , codex , or any command that reads a prompt on stdin. Without it, hand TASK.md to whatever you use. Proof, not vibes That port looked right but compared bytes instead of characters. 148 of 500 real calls caught it. On top of the recorded calls, fast-anything derives extra cases and lets the original answer them: edge cases (NaN, ±infinity, -0.0, zero and ±1, non-ASCII text, empty and up to 16× bigger inputs) and shrunk inputs (tiny and random slices). Nothing is enabled until every case matches: same values (floats within 1e-9), errors where the original errors. A port that is right but slower per call than the original (calling into Rust costs more than the work saved) isn't enabled either. FAST_ANYTHING_DISABLE=1 runs the original any time. Results Real runs on an i5-10500, Windows 11 (C and C++: a 4-core GitHub Actions Linux runner). Reproduce them from examples/ . app before after Python fuzzy dedupe (700 names) 4.91s 42ms, 116× TypeScript fuzzy dedupe (2,000 names) 3.11s 155ms, 20× PHP fuzzy dedupe (600 names) 2.94s 53ms, 55× Go fuzzy dedupe (3,000 names) 3.02s 144ms, 21× Ruby fuzzy dedupe (400 names) 3.13s 228ms, 14× C# fuzzy dedupe (4,000 names) 4.03s 312ms, 13× Java fuzzy dedupe (4,000 names) 3.50s 1.18s, 3× (11× on the function; the rest is JVM startup) C mandelbrot (8 zoom levels) 431ms 127ms, 3.4× C++ fuzzy dedupe (6,000 names) 3.02s 1.09s, 2.7× fast-anything ports the outermost loop it can, not the tiny function called inside it, so the app crosses into Rust once instead of millions of times. Porting only the inner levenshtein gave 35× and 1.9×. Why not rewrite it all? Compile time : each port is a one-function crate. Seconds, not minutes. Cache : every port shares one .fast/target . Delete it whenever you like. Risk : your code stays as it is. Rust is opt-in per function, checked against real behavior. abstract:
PcapAnalyzer Versión en español: README.es.md . Find the network fault in seconds, not hours. Upload a .pcap / .pcapng capture
(gzip too) and PcapAnalyzer tells you what is failing, why, and what to check next.
It runs on your own machine, so captures never leave your network. Free and open source (Apache 2.0). Status: beta. Try it without installing anything: https://pcap-analyzer-seven.vercel.app/#demo Download: https://sebaandrada6.gumroad.com/l/hspgx (free) or clone this repository. What it does 27 detectors that run on every capture, each with a severity and a next step: TCP: firewall blocks (SYN→RST), retransmissions, duplicate ACKs, loss and
reordering, zero and full windows, resets after the handshake, slow handshakes. Path: PMTUD black holes, low MSS, IP fragmentation, ICMP errors, routing loops. Name and address services: unanswered or slow DNS, SERVFAIL, NXDOMAIN bursts,
DHCP NAK / DECLINE / no answer, duplicate IPs, ARP storms. Applications: HTTP 4xx / 5xx and slow responses, TLS alerts, SSL 3.0 / TLS 1.0 / 1.1. Tunnels: IPsec (IKE and ESP), WireGuard, OpenVPN, GRE, L2TP and Teredo that are
one-way, never answer a handshake or keep renegotiating. Security: port scans and sweeps, cleartext logins (FTP, POP3, IMAP, SMTP AUTH,
HTTP Basic; credentials are never stored or shown), Telnet / SMBv1 / SNMP v1-v2c,
ARP spoofing, overlapping IP fragments. Capture quality first. It warns when the capture itself limits the result:
frames duplicated by a mirror port, traffic seen in one direction only, truncated
packets, connections already open when the capture started. Wireshark-style views: packet list with real Wireshark display filters over the
whole capture, colouring, CSV export, expert info, HTTP / DNS / DHCP / TLS tables,
response times and a flow diagram per conversation. AI investigation (optional): an AI investigates the capture with tools (real
filters, stream detail, statistics) and cites the packets behind every claim. You
can then ask follow-up questions. It uses your own Anthropic API key; without one, a
demo mode runs the full flow with text generated from the analysis, at no cost. PDF report , Spanish and English interface, light and dark theme. Quick start You need Docker with Docker Compose. On Windows, run the script from Git Bash or WSL. git clone https://github.com/sebaandrada-cell/PcapAnalyzer.git cd PcapAnalyzer
./start.sh The script creates a random access token (shown once, stored in .env ) and starts the
app. When the build finishes, open http://localhost:8080 , paste the token into the
"API token" field (top right) and upload a capture, or click "Try the sample capture". The app listens on 127.0.0.1 only. Do not expose it on a network without an
authenticated reverse proxy: the API can use your AI account. QUICKSTART.md has the details, the AI setup and troubleshooting. Without Docker You need Python 3.9+, Node 20+ and tshark (installed with Wireshark). cd backend
python3 -m venv .venv

npm install

encrypted (60 minutes of inactivity, or until you press "Delete capture now") and is
then deleted. The AI is optional. It only sees what its tools return (packet metadata; packet
content only if you switch it on for that session), never the pcap file. No telemetry and no accounts for the self-hosted version. title: Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs
abstract:
Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs Raph Levien, November 21, 2026 This is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs , published 4.5 years ago.
The world is different in many ways, but some of the advice there is still valid.
There have been roughly 20 Rust GUI toolkits announced since that blog post (see 2026 survey ), but also a recent rapid acceleration of interest in Rust GUI, fueled by AI. Rust GUI is still compelling The motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong.
Many shipping GUI apps suffer from poor performance, especially when built with cross-platform technology.
GUI toolkits shipped by platforms have largely stagnated, and system vendors remain uninterested in solving the cross-platform problem, so Electron has grown in popularity.
RAM remains expensive and the focus is shifting to mobile, so bloat has real consequences.
Building high-performance UI in Rust is a practical alternative. Adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow.
Few flagship apps use Rust for their UI.
One of the most notable is the Zed editor, built on their own GPUI framework.
It proves that shipping Rust UI is practical, and indeed, GPUI is emerging as a major choice for AI-driven rewrites, most notably Discord.
My personal sense is that GPUI is well suited to the Zed use case, and shipping in a real project boosts its visibility and credibility quite a bit, but it’s not necessarily the ideal choice for more general purpose applications.
Among other things, its 2D rendering engine is well suited to a text editor, but lacks full gradient support, blending, filters, and other features expected of a renderer in the same class as Vello or Skia. The reasons for slow adoption may be melting away.
Writing Rust code is harder than languages more traditionally used for UI (TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift), and finding engineers skilled in both Rust and UI is challenging.
But AI is changing the game.
There’s evidence that the LLM cost of writing Rust code is not significantly higher than other languages, and there is reason to believe that in large codebases, Rust will be more maintainable because its type system helps enforce invariants.
So if all languages have roughly the same cost, then why not go with one that has a dramatically better combination of safety and performance? For these reasons, Rust is rapidly becoming the language for AI rewrites of existing codebases.
But there is still no consensus on the strategy for the UI layer.
I predict there will be a small explosion of trying lots of different things. Native is complicated My 2022 blog post had a large section on “native,” first pointing out that the term has no clear meaning, and more broadly pointing out that “native” UI toolkits are simply choices among many, and should be evaluated on the important quality criteria. I think this is largely still true, but it depends greatly on which platform is being targeted.
Windows still has no clear native choice (see Microsoft Hasn’t Had a Coherent GUI Strategy Since Petzold ) and on Mac there is a bit of fragmentation between AppKit and SwiftUI.
However, SwiftUI has performance issues (see Michael Tsai blog from 2025 ) and so it is clearly possible to do better on the performance front. While desktop UI has remained stagnant, the situation on mobile is a bit different.
Platforms continue to invest, and there are many fine details that are important for an app to look and feel native.
One very notable example is Liquid Glass on iOS – if you use UIKit or SwiftUI, you can get that with little effort, but apps built with cross-platform toolkits won’t quite seem right.
In addition, making gesture recognition, scroll dynamics, and IME 100% match the platform are not yet fully solved problems. Thus, for mobile, an extremely viable path is to use the native toolkit for UI but do the common “business logic” in Rust.
I’m not sure about the business logic, but for the UI, this is the decision that Shopify has made recently, abandoning React Native.
I believe 1Password has this architecture.
This is also the "Phoenix" plan for Discord on mobile, while using GPUI on desktop. That said, there's been considerable progress in trying to build mobile UI entirely in Rust.
Below is a short screencast of the editor demo in android-view .
You can see that a lot of IME functionality works, including swiping, moving the cursor by rolling the space bar, and deleting in semantic chunks.
Not shown in the video below, but composition regions (needed for CJK) also work, and there's basic accessibility through AccessKit. Text layout and accessibility infrastructure is basically solved One of the big unsolved problems as of the 2022 blog post was text layout.
It is of course a hard problem to get right.
I’m pleased to say that the ecosystem now has a good solution, in the form of Parley .
It’s gotten there as a result of sustained investment from Google, Canva, and Dioxus (now Cognition), as well as contributions from the community.
It seems to be used in the majority of new Rust UI toolkits.
In addition, to help mitigate the risk of monoculture, Cosmic Text is a viable alternative. AccessKit was just getting started in 2022, but is now solid infrastructure as well, and used by most UI toolkits.
I should note, though, there is a difference between a good integration and a box ticking exercise.
And there is more work to be done, for example to make rich text editing fully accessible.
One other problem I'd like to see addressed is performance degradation when accessibility is enabled.
This is a problem for egui in particular, as it has to build and diff a tree each animation frame, undercutting the benefits of its underlying immediate mode design. System compositor is still unsolved One topic I talked about extensively in the 2022 blog post is leveraging the system compositor.
This issue is even more pressing today, especially with the increased importance of video.
You really want a video playing in a hardware accelerated layer when possible, and on low end devices it’s the only hope for getting smooth frame rates. There has been some progress, notably the subduction library, but it certainly isn’t commonly integrated into UI toolkits yet.
To do it well is a challenging problem, as the capabilities provided by the platform vary widely.
Ideally there’s a rich and high level interface, something like CALayer on Apple platforms, and polyfills to implement that interface as well as possible on other platforms.
On Android, when the task is something simple, like overlaying some GUI controls on a video, it would use SurfaceFlinger layers, but when it involves more sophisticated compositing, it would run shaders on the GPU. This is absolutely something we should build, ideally as a high quality community project rather than something with dozens of vibe-coded forks.
But even in the latter case it’s better for it to exist than not. Immediate vs retained mode One of the challenges of the Rust UI ecosystem is that different applications have different needs.
The idea of a single, unified UI for completely general purpose use may be behind us, especially now that LLMs can optimize and fine tune for specific use cases. That’s been playing out architecturally in the choice between immediate mode and retained mode.
Immediate mode is very appealing because it’s less total code and seems quite a bit simpler.
And for some applications (most especially development support for games) it works well.
However, I am concerned it won’t scale especially well.
In short, it’s good at the first 90%, but it makes the second 90% harder.
To be considered really production-ready, it has to establish stable widget identities to build and update the accessibility tree, and it has to reliably cache expensive intermediate artifacts such as text layouts (simple immediate mode often gets around this by cutting corners in text layout, which may be fine for gamedev).

title: 87% of the Anthropic power will come from gas and 11% from coal in 2028
abstract:
In The AI Gas Rush: Risks and Implications of “Bring Your Own Power” , we dug into how data centers are increasingly securing their own dedicated primary power generation rather than relying solely on utilities to procure power (“BYOP”). We identified 177 GW of planned BYOP gas capacity—enough to power 65% of all US homes. Conversely, we found renewables are much less common than gas for BYOP: we estimate that for current proposals, less than 20% of energy generation will come from renewable sources by 2032. But BYOP projects aren’t the only new fossil sources that are coming online to meet the skyrocketing energy demands of AI data centers. Another 200 GW of new fossil power plants is being built on the grid to meet growing demand, due in large part to data centers. 1 As a case study of how the AI buildout is driving both new BYOP and grid fossil infrastructure, we analyzed the compute commitments of a single company: Anthropic. Map of Anthropic’s data centers and associated power plants. See our full dataset for details of each site. Figure 1. Breakdown of power source for Anthropic’s compute. Finding 1: Anthropic has made no direct commitments to renewable energy in the U.S. Though Anthropic has stated “We’re also working to broaden our energy mix with geothermal, wind, solar, and emerging technologies”, its only publicly disclosed commitments, contract, or investments in renewable power are in Norway and Canada (as of November 2026). In contrast, Anthropic is directly procuring fossil power equipment—it recently “ bought commitments for 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty [gas] generators for $3.4bn ”. Finding 2: Anthropic’s currently contracted data centers in the U.S. will be overwhelmingly powered by fossil fuels in the near term. By considering on-site gas and the grid power plants which are likely to meet Anthropic’s added load (i.e. marginal generators), we estimate about 87% of the company’s power will come from gas and 11% from coal in 2028. As of October 2026, Anthropic has contracted 15 GW of compute ; of this, about 5.9–9.6 GW is contracted to specific data center sites. For a sense of scale, 9.6 GW could power about 7 million homes or cover 18% of the peak power demand of California —the world’s 4 th largest economy. This demand will be met with a mix of new on-site gas, new grid gas, and existing grid gas, coal, and nuclear. In the short term, no grid renewables are attributed to Anthropic’s power use, because—without commitments to new renewable capacity—new load on the grid will be met by dispatchable, marginal fossil resources. 2 For more details, see our full dataset and our methodology below. Figure 2. Anthropic’s emissions from power consumption expected in 2028. Emissions for Google, Microsoft, and Meta are annual Scope 2, location-based emissions from their most recent sustainability reports. California power sector emissions are for all power plants operating within the state (source: EIA ). Finding 3: Total CO 2 emissions from Anthropic’s power use at these sites could reach 17–38 million MtCO 2 e per year in 2028 , when this capacity is expected to be online. This range reflects uncertainty in Anthropic’s average power use, due to factors such as cooling needs and average utilization (see methodology below). In our mid-case, Anthropic will emit 32 million MtCO 2 e in 2028. These totals will continue to grow—possibly doubling by 2030, as some analysts expect Anthropic to secure 30 GW by 2030 . To put these figures in context, Anthropic’s CO 2 emissions from power use in 2028: could exceed the emissions of all of California’s power generation ( 31.1 MMtCO 2 e in 2024 , not including imports). could exceed Meta, Microsoft, and Google’s combined Scope 2 emissions from 2025 (their location-based emissions, before renewable energy offsets, were 5.9 million , 12 million and 15 million MtCO 2 e, respectively) 3 would represent a 16–36% increase over 2024 levels of the entire U.S. data center sector ( 105 MMtCO 2 e ). would increase the entire U.S.’s power sector emissions ( 1,485 MMtCO 2 e in 2025 ) by 1.1–2.5%. Finding 4: Anthropic’s data centers are sited in areas where the grid mainly uses coal and gas. We estimate the average carbon intensity of Anthropic’s power to be 1,033–1,076 lb CO 2 e/MWh, 35% higher than the U.S. grid average ( 767 lb CO 2 e/MWh ). 4 Figure 3. CO 2 e and NOx emissions factors for on-site and grid power serving each of Anthropic’s data center sites. Finding 5: 80% of on-site power uses inefficient simple cycle turbines and engines. About 25% (2.5 GW) of Anthropic’s contracted power will come from on-site, behind-the-meter gas. 80% of this on-site capacity consists of inefficient simple cycle turbines and engines, which emit more pollution per unit of electricity than modern combined cycle plants (see our report for more details on the types of power generation being used for on-site gas). Finding 6: Based on EPA’s nationally-averaged benefit-per-ton estimates , air pollution from Anthropic’s on-site and grid power use could cause $2–3 billion in annual health damages , with total emissions of over 13,000 tons per year (tpy) of nitrogen oxides (NOx) and 2,000 tpy of fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ). In October 2026, Anthropic outlined its “ approach to responsible data center development ”, stating: “We follow the air permitting process everywhere we operate and require the same of the plants powering our data centers. Those plants must also use emissions control technology, including selective catalytic reduction [SCR].” However, Anthropic has used compute capacity at SpaceX’s Colossus 2 facility since May 2026 , which still receives most of its power from temporary, unpermitted turbines , the majority of which are not equipped with SCR. Anthropic will use as much as 600 MW of power from Colossus 2 by the end of 2026 (see methodology below). Anthropic has also contracted 460 MW (and is in talks for up to 920 MW ) of power from Nscale’s Monarch Compute Campus in Mason, West Virginia. This facility will be powered by inefficient reciprocating engines which have significant formaldehyde and hazardous air pollutant (HAP) emissions compared to conventional gas power plants. For more, see our full dataset on Anthropic’s compute and our report on BYOP . Methodology We gathered details about Anthropic’s data center commitments from Epoch AI’s tracker , Anthropic’s announcements and filings , announcements and filings from partners (including Amazon and SpaceX ), and reporting from The Information , Semafor , and others. We first identified the source for each data center’s power. For projects with on-site gas (Monarch, Nexus, Colossus 2) or new grid gas (including indirectly contracted projects such as the Schahfer expansion for the AWS New Carlisle site and Entergy Mississippi’s gas plants for AWS’s Madison and Ridgeland facilities) we used emissions factors from permits where available, or permit values from comparable facilities. For grid-connected facilities without associated new generation capacity, we assume these sites will be powered by marginal, dispatchable grid capacity. We used EPA’s AVERT tool to model which power plants would meet the new incremental load from Anthropic’s facilities based on each site’s expected power use and region. AVERT uses historical EPA data for these power plants to model the expected short-run marginal emissions rate of CO 2 and criteria pollutants (NO x , PM 2.5 , etc.). We use AVERT because we are interested in the short-term impacts from new data centers coming online in the next several years. To calculate the amount of power used by each site, and in turn the total quantity of air pollutant emissions, we assumed power usage effectiveness (PUE) ranges from 1.1–1.2 for all sites (typical values for hyperscale data centers are between 1.05–1.3), and power utilization ranges from 60–80%.

title: Notes on the discrete Fourier transform (DFT)
abstract:
In the previous post on this
topic ,
we’ve seen how the Discrete-Time Fourier Series (DTFS) and transform
(DTFT) are used to analyze infinite-duration periodic and non-periodic
discrete signals. Now, it’s time to turn to realistic digital signal
processing where signals are not only discrete, but also finite in
duration . Analyzing signal samples Suppose we have N samples of a signal - it’s a list of N numbers: \[x[n]\qquad n\in\{0..N-1\}\] We want to analyze the frequencies present in this signal; in other
words, to find the coefficients in a series of complex exponentials that
reconstructs the signal. One option is to assume that x[n] is an
infinite domain signal with zero values outside our N samples, and then
compute its DTFT: \[X(w)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}x[n]e^{-i w n}\\\] However, this is a continuous function of frequency w , so it’s
difficult compute on an actual computer; we cannot evaluate and
store it for all w , so we have to choose which w to compute it
for. We'll soon see how this choice is made. The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) But there's an alternative way to look at the problem. We only have N samples of the signal x , so we can assume they represent a single period
of a periodic signal. And in that case, we can use DTFS; recall that the
coefficients of the series are: \[a_k=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-ik(2\pi/N)n}\] As we’ve seen in the post on the DTFS ,
this series can be used to
reconstruct a discrete, periodic signal precisely . Since our signal x[n] is finite and we assume it’s just one period of a periodic
signal, it means we can also reconstruct x[n] precisely using a
DTFS. This is the main insight behind the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT).
First, by convention [1] we define: \[X[k]=Na_k\] And then: \[\boxed{
X[k]=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-ik(2\pi/N)n}
}\] This is called the Discrete Fourier Transform of x[n] . The term transform may be a bit puzzling here - after all, we’re just using the
series coefficients - so isn’t it more proper to just say series ?
Perhaps, though in mathematics a transform has a pretty general
meaning of "a mapping that takes a mathematical object and produces
another object"; in that sense, "transform" is proper here because we
take an object - x[n] and produce another object - X[k] . Moreover, DFT and DTFT are intimately related. Recall how we said
earlier that the DTFT is tricky to compute because w is a
continuous variable? Well, the DFT gives us a way to sample that
variable into the discrete domain: \[X_{DFT}[k]=X_{DTFT}(2\pi k/N)\] So the DFT can be seen as exactly N equally spaced samples of
the DTFT. Computing the DFT Since the goal of this post is specifically to demonstrate computable methods of applying Fourier analysis to discrete digital signals, here’s
the Python code to calculate the DFT of a signal: def dft ( x ): """Return X[k] = sum_n x[n] exp(-2 pi i k n / N).""" N = len ( x ) n = np . arange ( N ) X = np . empty ( N , dtype = complex ) for k in range ( N ): weights = np . exp ( - 2 j * np . pi * k * n / N ) X [ k ] = np . sum ( x * weights ) return X It shouldn’t be hard to see the correspondence between this code and the
mathematical formula for X[k] . Python’s Numpy code is vectorized
by default, so the weights array is computed in whole for every k (because n is an array of indices [0..N-1] ). DFT and the complex roots of unity In my earlier post on the complex roots of
unity ,
we’ve seen how powers of the roots of unity form an orthogonal basis for \mathbb{C}^n . Now let’s show the beautiful theoretical
connection between this fact and the DFT. Recall that the N -th roots of unity can be written as: \[z_k=e^{i2\pi k/N},\qquad k=0,1,\dots,N-1\] Since all z_k are just powers of w=z_1=e^{i2\pi/N} , we
can write them as: \[z_k=w^k,\qquad k=0,1,\dots,N-1\] The conjugates of the roots of unity are roots of unity themselves: \[z_k^*=e^{-i2\pi k/N},\qquad k=0,1,\dots,N-1\] With z_k^* being the same as z_{N-k} , so when we
enumerate all the roots of unity, we’re also enumerating their
conjugates, just in a reversed order. With that in mind, let’s denote [2] \omega=z_1^*=e^{-i2\pi/N} ,
and examine the sequence: \[\mu_N=\left[1,\omega,\omega^2,\dots,\omega^{N-1} \right]\] The vectors formed by (element-wise) raising \mu_N to integer powers
from 0 to N-1 can be collected into a matrix: \[F=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\ 1 & \omega & \omega^2 & \cdots & \omega^{N-1} \\ 1 & \omega^2 & \omega^4 & \cdots & \omega^{2(N-1)} \\ \vdots & & & & \vdots \\ 1 & \omega^{N-1} & \omega^{2(N-1)} & \cdots & \omega^{(N-1)(N-1)} \\
\end{bmatrix}\] In the roots of unity
post ,
we’ve proven that the rows of this matrix form an orthogonal basis over \mathbb{C}^N . In other words, any vector in \mathbb{C}^N can be represented as a linear combination of the rows of F . title: C-MoA-XRT: Explainability-Aware Trust Routing for Collaborative Threat Detection in Mobile-Edge Networks
abstract: Threat detection in mobile-edge networks requires reliable inference from heterogeneous telemetry whose availability and evidential quality may vary over time. LLM-assisted detectors further introduce uncertainty because prediction confidence may not reflect evidence trustworthiness, while collaborative reasoning can amplify unsupported decisions. This paper proposes C-MoA-XRT, a trust-aware collaborative Mixture-of-Agents framework for resilient mobile-edge threat detection. C-MoA-XRT distributes complementary network evidence across specialized LLM agents and performs event-specific trust routing before collaborative inference. The proposed routing mechanism separates prediction confidence from decision authority by assessing the reliability, consistency, and evidential support of each specialist output. A defensive red-team reasoning stage subsequently examines the fused evidence, while an evidence-anchored decision firewall constrains unstable collaborative reasoning from overriding the calibrated detection outcome. Experiments on NF-UNSW-NB15 show that C-MoA-XRT achieves an F1 score of 0.900 with full attack recall and reduces the false-positive rate by approximately 75% relative to the evaluated single-agent RAG+LLM baseline. Under measurement drift, trust-aware evidence gating improves PR-AUC from 0.694 to 0.917 over confidence-based routing, while maintaining resilience under the evaluated telemetry-dropout and unreliable-specialist conditions. These results demonstrate that explicit control of evidence trust and reasoning authority can improve the robustness of collaborative LLM-based threat detection in mobile-edge networks.

title: LLM-Enabled Self-Organizing UAV Networks for Autonomous Service Provisioning
abstract: The growing demand for flexible and resilient low-altitude connectivity is driving UAV networks toward increasingly autonomous operation. However, existing approaches often assume known user distributions, fixed network configurations, or treat exploration, access, and backhaul separately, resulting in a gap between user discovery and end-to-end service in initially unknown environments. To address this challenge, we propose a self-organizing heterogeneous UAV networking framework, referred to as Discovery-to-Service (D2S) Network, that supports the complete process from user discovery to end-to-end service provisioning. The framework adopts a dual-timescale coordination mechanism: at the fast timescale, onboard graph reinforcement learning agents perform user exploration and local control, while at the slower timescale, a basestation-hosted LLM reconfigures the access and backhaul infrastructure based on discovered demands and the global network state. Experiments over 42 scenarios show that, compared with a heuristic connectivity-constrained grid-greedy method, the proposed framework improves effective coverage by 23.38 percentage points, terminal throughput by 55.3%, and cumulative throughput by 44.3%, demonstrating its effectiveness for autonomous network formation under unknown demand.

title: An Agentic AI Architecture for Zero-Touch IoT Device Onboarding and Interoperability
abstract: The heterogeneity of Internet of Things (IoT) devices remains a major barrier to scalable deployment, automated onboarding, and cross-platform interoperability. Device-specific protocols, software dependencies, telemetry formats, and runtime constraints often require manual configuration and ad-hoc integration logic. This paper proposes an agentic AI architecture for zero-touch IoT device onboarding, where a large language model is used as an autonomous configuration agent capable of generating device-side software, installing dependencies, validating runtime behavior, and recursively correcting failures until convergence is achieved. The proposed architecture introduces a closed-loop workflow that combines device inspection, AI-based runtime generation, remote deployment, telemetry validation, and self-correction. Interoperability is addressed through a normalized telemetry contract that abstracts device-specific behavior into a common telemetry representation. We evaluate the approach on a real IoT device by benchmarking multiple AI models under clean installation conditions in two campaigns: the original pipeline and a second pipeline assisted by a locally trained semantic context optimizer. The comparison covers convergence time, correction cycles, recursive iterations, and prompt tokens. The optimizer-assisted campaign reduced prompt redundancy and recursive recovery effort while preserving successful onboarding across all tested models. Overall, the results show that agentic AI can support zero-touch onboarding while exposing measurable differences among models in reliability, efficiency, and runtime convergence.

title: Ripple: Coordination-Free Message Scheduling for Multi-Agent LLM Workflows at the IoT Edge
abstract: Distributed intelligence in IoT and edge systems increasingly runs as agentic AI: production large language model (LLM) applications execute as workflows—directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of agents and tools that exchange prompts, retrieved context, and tool outputs across end devices, edge servers, and the cloud. When many such workflows share a capacity-limited link, such as an edge gateway uplink or a regional aggregation point, that link rather than the GPU gates the communication phase, and a message that unblocks an idle agent may wait behind an unrelated bulk transfer. A dependency-aware link scheduler can mitigate this, but a scheduler that ranks messages by whole-workflow remaining work and downstream critical path requires a global, continuously updated view of every concurrent workflow, that is, a central coordinator that heterogeneous and dynamic IoT edge deployments typically lack. This paper presents Ripple, a coordination-free link scheduler in which each agent ranks only its own outgoing messages, using a local rule that prioritizes downstream criticality per unit transmission cost and applies an age credit to curb long waits. The required downstream-criticality signal is a bounded scalar initialized with the source's task descriptor, so no runtime node maintains the global graph. In an event-driven, flow-level evaluation on a shared 100 Mbps link with heavy-tailed messages (median 419 KB, 99th-percentile about 30 MB) and four DAG shapes, network waiting accounts for 46% of the mean workflow completion time (WCT) under fair sharing at offered load ρ=0.88. Ripple reduces mean and 99th-percentile WCT by 24% and 38% relative to fair sharing, and attains 9% lower mean and 27% lower tail WCT than a global-view reference heuristic while using no global state. A knowledge-horizon analysis shows that performance saturates at a one-hop view, and an ablation finds that message size and age drive most of the aggregate gain. The results use an idealized flow-level priority model; a DSCP/eBPF realization that needs no coordinator and no change to the LLM runtime is proposed but not yet evaluated.

title: MOSAIC: Efficient Collaborative Inference for Multi-Modal Large Language Models with Distributed Edge Computing
abstract: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) enable natural language reasoning over heterogeneous sensory data, appealing to many edge AI scenarios, yet their deployment faces competing demands on latency, energy, and quality. We present MOSAIC, which adopts a component-level decomposition and distributed deployment paradigm for efficient MLLM inference at the edge, realizing three core ideas: parallel encoding, token pruning, and device-server collaboration. Specifically, for the offline stage, modality-specific encoders distilled from a unified foundation model are co-deployed with Q-Former projection on edge devices for parallel encoding, while LoRA instruction fine-tuning adapts the frozen LLM backbone to downstream tasks. For the online stage, we formulate a multi-objective optimization over latency and energy that jointly tunes token budgets, device frequencies, and quantization precision under long-term semantic accuracy constraints, achieving dynamic token pruning and device-server collaboration. We leverage Lagrangian relaxation to decompose the original problem into tractable per-slot subproblems and design an online algorithm with provable near-optimal performance and guaranteed constraint satisfaction. We implement a realistic testbed for extensive performance evaluation, which demonstrates that MOSAIC reduces latency by up to 49.8% and energy by up to 65.1% over advanced baselines while maintaining high semantic accuracy.

title: Model-based Zero-shot Conflict Detection Framework via Gradients in O-RAN
abstract: Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) enables network control through multi-vendor xApps operating both within and across layers, subnets, and domains, whose concurrent execution can trigger conflicts that are latent during the development phase. Existing conflict management approaches rely heavily on joint-execution data, which is often unavailable in practice. To address this limitation, we formalize a novel problem termed conflict reasoning, which involves identifying conflict-inducing conditions given only marginal datasets from each individual xApp. We propose ZODIAC, a three-stage framework for zero-shot conflict condition inference that comprises uncertainty-aware surrogate model training, trajectory-level diffusion training, and compositional guided denoising for efficient, physics-constrained, and reliable condition search. We derive a theoretical lower confidence bound showing that the compositional reasoning in ZODIAC serves as a principled surrogate for true conflict severity, with the epistemic penalty directly controlling the approximation gap. We evaluate ZODIAC on both the lightweight Mobile-Env platform across all three O-RAN Alliance conflict types (direct, indirect, and implicit) and a realistic NS-O-RAN-Flexric simulator. ZODIAC consistently outperforms baseline condition search methods, achieving over 20% higher True Positive Rate at Top-20, substantially stronger Spearman rank correlation, greater scenario diversity, and competitive computational efficiency. Ablation studies confirm the necessity of each guidance component, with epistemic uncertainty penalties proving essential for filtering spurious conflicts. To the best of our knowledge, ZODIAC is the first framework in O-RAN that enables conflict reasoning from marginal offline data without requiring any joint-execution traces.

title: Demo: Multimodal Stress Monitoring with Split Federated Fine-Tuning on Mobile Devices
abstract: We present an end-to-end mobile system for proactive stress monitoring from wearable signals. The framework is supported by an extensible split federated learning system that enables on-device LoRA fine-tuning of large language models. By analyzing physiological data, the application distinguishes emotional states, summarizes recent trends, and provides brief, actionable suggestions. Upon detecting a negative emotional state, the paired smartwatch or smartphone proactively delivers notifications to users to encourage mindfulness. The on-site demonstration will showcase real-time sensing-inference on smartwatch-phone pairs, alongside a recorded split federated learning process that continuously learns from user private data. Our code has been open-sourced at: https://github.com/HKU-WILL-Lab/Multimodal-Stress-Monitoring-with-Split-Federated-Fine-Tuning-on-Mobile-Devices.

title: TrustSense: Structure-Adaptive Trust Inference for Resilient Cooperative IoT Sensing
abstract: Cooperative IoT sensing must assess reports from noisy, faulty, or compromised devices despite churn and changing inter-device relationships. We present TrustSense, a structure-adaptive GNN framework for per-report trust evaluation. TrustSense represents active devices as a dynamic graph and maps each report's neighborhood-based reconstruction residual to a trust score. A layer-wise soft edge mask downweights less informative dependencies, while forced anchor attention reserves a controlled share of attention for available trusted anchors. At runtime, historical consistency drives anchor-rooted credit diffusion to prioritize returning devices, and accepted reports guide subsequent evaluations. Shared GNN parameters make TrustSense inductive, enabling targeted adaptation to unseen devices without usable history. TrustSense is also location-centric, device-agnostic, and prior-free with respect to the sensing process, assuming neither a parametric sensing-value distribution nor a known propagation model. We evaluate TrustSense on synthetic RF data and real LoED traces with injected attacks. With 10% additive-bias attackers on LoED, it improves F1 by 4.25× over the strongest evaluated baseline and achieves a lower Brier score. These gains persist with up to 50% malicious devices, while inference latency remains within 230-250 ms at several thousand devices.

title: Poster: ProbeGuard, Budgeted Active Probing for Safe LLM Service Recomposition under Silent Semantic Drift
abstract: Under silent semantic drift, an upgraded edge-cloud service stays schema-compatible but changes a unit, precondition, or state transition, invalidating LLM-orchestrated compositions. ProbeGuard treats candidate behaviors as a version space and spends a small budget of safe probes to discriminate them; owner-protected executable clauses cannot be weakened by an LLM, and a service is cleared only when all evidence-compatible hypotheses agree. In 252 controlled episodes, hybrid hypothesis generation recovers 94.8% of drifted behaviors, and ProbeGuard automates 98.4% of decisions correctly while cutting harmful clearance from 5.3% to 2.7% and latency from 0.94 to 0.56 s versus the strongest deployable baseline.

title: Query-Aware Temporal Evidence Prefetching to Support Communication-Efficient Video AIoT Reasoning
abstract: Video Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) systems increasingly use vision-language models (VLMs) to answer questions about dynamic scenes, yet continuous high-resolution streaming may exceed wireless and latency budgets. We therefore study a layered setting in which the receiver always holds a low-resolution stream and requests only a limited number of high-resolution enhancement patches. Within this setting, we propose query-aware temporal semantic prefetching (QTPF), which uses the task query and prior low-resolution images to predict evidence locations in the next sampled observation before it arrives. On 14,913 LingoQA scenery questions, QTPF obtains 0.6355 Recall@5 under an OpenCLIP evidence target, compared with 0.5858 for a query-only learned model and 0.6270 for an independently trained query-aware last-frame predictor. The advantage persists under independently generated SigLIP targets, where QTPF obtains 0.5473 against 0.5328 for the last-frame predictor. With five enhancement patches, the delivered JPEG payload averages 9.77 KB, which is 20.9% below the 12.35 KB full-resolution image, and the predictor adds only 0.75 ms on an RTX 6000 Ada GPU.

title: Poster: When Safer AI Makes the System Less Safe: Inference Reuse and Systemic Risk in Networked Autonomy
abstract: Network-assisted inference can improve the decisions of autonomous agents, while reusing inference results can avoid repeated computation. However, when multiple agents reuse the same inference result, their failures become more coupled. We show that beyond a simple threshold, simultaneous failure can become more likely even though every agent is individually more accurate. We then characterize when the resource savings from reuse justify this added shared-failure risk.

title: MIRA: An Edge-Cloud Multimodal LLM Framework for DESH Assessment in IoT-Enabled MRI Workflows
abstract: Connected MRI scanners operate as networked medical devices within DICOM-based healthcare Internet of Things (IoT) workflows, but conventional connectivity primarily moves images to a Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS) rather than adding task-specific reasoning near acquisition. Building on DESH-App 2.0, a preceding machine-learning contribution accepted for oral presentation at SIN Firenze 2026, this paper specifies MIRA (Multimodal Imaging Reasoning and Assessment), a vendor-neutral edge-cloud module for assessing disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid spaces (DESH). A hospital-edge gateway validates and de-identifies 3D T1-weighted DICOM studies, derives ventricular, high-convexity, and Sylvian-fissure masks with SegFormer3D, and converts each volume into a compact evidence package comprising 12 representative slices with overlays, 17 global, zonal, and ratio features, and quality-control tokens. LLaVA-Med-7B and Lingshu-7B are adapted through 4-bit QLoRA to return constrained JSON containing class, confidence, named anatomical evidence, and an abstention or quality warning. The edge-cloud partition keeps raw volumes inside the institutional network; only the compact evidence package may reach an authenticated inference service, while structured outputs return to the PACS workstation. The evaluation protocol jointly covers diagnostic discrimination, calibration, evidence agreement, unsupported claims, abstention, latency, transmitted bytes, memory demand, link-loss recovery, and multi-device interoperability. MIRA is designed to add auditable multimodal reasoning to connected MRI workflows without modifying safety-critical scanner controls.

title: Reliable V2X-Enabled Autonomous Driving with Explainable Federated Neuro-Symbolic Intelligence
abstract: Connected and autonomous vehicles rely on vehicle-to-everything (V2X) cooperation when local sensing is incomplete or delayed, as often occurs in dense traffic, occluded intersections, and roads with constrained communication. Yet many data-driven driving models remain difficult to interpret, and centralized learning requires large raw sensory data transfers that raise communication and privacy concerns. This paper proposes an explainable federated neuro-symbolic intelligence framework for reliable V2X-enabled autonomous driving. The framework combines neural perception, symbolic rule-based reasoning, fuzzy uncertainty modeling, and reliability-aware federated learning. Each vehicle trains a local decision agent from local driving and communication-context observations, while an edge or roadside unit aggregates model updates without collecting raw sensory data. The local agent also produces an interpretable rationale, including activated rules, uncertainty indicators, and risk factors associated with the selected decision. Simulation-based V2X results show that the proposed method improves decision quality, reduces missed safety-critical states, and converges faster than standard Federated Averaging (FedAvg) under vehicle-side data that are not independent and identically distributed (non-IID).

title: FrozenSFL: Model-Frozen Split Federated Learning for Resource-Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning over Heterogeneous Edge Devices
abstract: Collaborative fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) at the network edge enables privacy-preserving and personalized generative intelligence, but is constrained by the limited memory and compute resources of edge devices. Traditional approaches, such as split federated learning (SFL), partition models between devices and a server, requiring iterative exchanges of activations/gradients while the server manages multiple submodels. This leads to substantial communication overhead, high activation storage costs, and severe server-side memory pressure when scaling to massive heterogeneous devices. In this paper, we propose FrozenSFL, a resource-efficient SFL framework for collaborative fine-tuning of LLMs across heterogeneous edge devices. At its core, FrozenSFL strictly freezes device-side submodels to eliminate both deviceside backpropagation and server-to-device gradient transmission, thereby removing on-device activation storage requirements and downlink communication overhead. Building upon this design, we improve the framework in two aspects. First, we design a layerwise LoRA aggregation strategy to handle structural heterogeneity introduced by device-specific model partitioning and enable efficient server-side updates. Second, we introduce a server-side feature caching mechanism that reuses invariant features, allowing subsequent training epochs to proceed offline and reducing redundant computation and communication. We implement the FrozenSFL system as an asynchronous multi-threaded pipeline, which serves as our real-world testbed for evaluation. On the device side, forward computation and data transmission are decoupled via a producer-consumer mechanism. On the server side, a first-in-first-out scheduling strategy serializes fine-tuning tasks across devices. A hybrid memory-disk streaming mechanism further buffers incoming data and ensures stable training under network variability. Extensive evaluations with representative models, including BERT-Base (0.11B), ViT-Large (0.3B), and LLaMA-2-7B (7B), validate the effectiveness of FrozenSFL. In particular, for LLaMA-2-7B, FrozenSFL can reduce device/server VRAM footprint by up to 14%/82.7% with only 1% accuracy loss, while achieving up to 6.7× fine-tuning speedup.

title: Demo: On-Device Agent for Personalized and Efficient Mobile Network Configuration
abstract: As mobile devices increasingly operate across heterogeneous access networks and diverse usage contexts, efficient network configuration requires decisions that adapt to both dynamic network conditions and individual user preferences. We demonstrate an on-device communication agent that transforms historical user network-switching behavior into personalized configuration rules. An on-device Large language model (LLM) analyzes switching records offline and generates condition-action rules capturing recurring user preferences. During real-time use, the agent retrieves matched rules locally and executes the corresponding network configuration after user confirmation, without invoking the LLM. Attendees will choose a prepared behavior trace, inspect the rule generated on the phone, and recreate its triggering context to observe an immediate network switch. The demonstration shows how separating deliberation from execution makes personalized mobile network configuration both interpretable and responsive while keeping user data and inference on the device.

title: Your Palm Is in My Hand: Palm-Vein Biometric Spoofing via Electromagnetic Side Channel
abstract: As a biometric modality, palm-vein authentication has seen growing adoption in recent years and is becoming prevalent in wallet-free payments and critical access-control applications. Although palm-vein patterns are widely regarded as nearly impossible to forge or steal, our study reveals that electromagnetic emanations induced during sensor operation can leak information correlated with a user's palm-vein characteristics, enabling attackers to reconstruct palm-vein images and spoof authentication systems. In this paper, we present PVSpy, a novel attack framework that demonstrates the feasibility of this attack. Specifically, PVSpy passively captures electromagnetic emanations radiated from palm-vein sensors, extracts features that map the captured signals to palm-vein images, and exploits diffusion models for biometric reconstructions to spoof palm-vein authentication devices. We extensively evaluate PVSpy on five commercial devices, and the recovered vein patterns exhibit a promising level of similarity. In addition, we conduct 30 end-to-end spoofing attacks against these commercial-off-the-shelf devices with different types of palm-vein sensors, and PVSpy achieves 26.7% (top-1) and 63.3% (top-3) success rates.
